text:
I


Let the red carnation sleep

or the white jasmine of the temples;

for the thistle is only disdain,

and the laurel only fury.

Let the altar boy give his honey,

and the wrinkled orange

and the thirsty pomegranate

juice and blood—gold and ruby;

for I prefer you to them,

little purple poppy.



II


At the foot of the leafy fig tree

the little carpet spreads its mantle;

the simple anacua grows,

and the courtly rose;

where the butterfly does not,

the hummingbird turns it iridescent.

But I prefer you,

whose hand draws away:

vessel in which sleeps the lament

of the valley where I was born.



III


When day is reborn

and the siesta awakens,

the magpies celebrate

with salvos of clamor,

why, poppy, so cold,

or so pure, or so silent?

Why, without telling me anything,

do you fill me with an uncertain longing—

an exhausted cup, an open hand—

if you are not in love?



IV


Will golden stars be born

from your trembling chalice—

a rule for thought

or a little box for tears?

No sonorous song is worth

the silence I heard from you.

I am testing in you

how much music errs.

Poppy of my land:

fall in love with me.

translation.title: Gloss of My Land
translation.editorial_note: “Anacua,” “bujeta,” and the local flowers are retained or rendered cautiously; “bujeta” is translated as a small box while preserving the source’s uncertainty.
